reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Control Flow & Decision Making
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 2. Python becomes much more useful once it can make decisions and repeat work automatically.

Up to this point, most of our code has simply run from top to bottom. Now we’ll give Python rules: if something is true, do one thing; otherwise, do something else. We’ll also use loops so one block of code can process many values.

[tts-break]

These ideas are the foundation for tasks such as classifying records, counting cases, applying business rules, and summarizing a dataset.

slides.title: What changes after Module 1?
slides.transcript:
Module 1 focused on values, calculations, and output. The big change now is that Python can choose a path.

A condition asks a True or False question. A branch is the block of code that runs when a condition is satisfied. A loop repeats a block of work. Loop control changes when that repetition stops or skips.

[tts-break]

Think of the workflow as data value, condition, action, then the next value. That simple structure is behind a surprising amount of analytics logic.

slides.title: Learning path for this session
slides.transcript:
We’ll build control flow in a logical order. First come Boolean conditions. Then we’ll use if, elif, and else to choose among outcomes.

After that, for loops let us repeat over known items, while loops repeat while a condition remains true, and finally we combine these ideas in common analytics patterns such as classification, counting, and flagging.

[tts-break]

As you work through the examples, do not just ask whether the code runs. Ask which condition becomes true, which block executes, and how the values change from one repetition to the next.

slides.title: A condition asks a True/False question
slides.transcript:
A condition is simply a question that Python can answer with True or False.

Sales greater than target asks whether one number is larger than another. Status equal to Open asks whether two values match exactly. Returns not equal to zero asks whether a value is different from zero.

[tts-break]

The comparison operators in the table are worth recognizing: double equals compares equality, exclamation equals means not equal, and the greater-than and less-than symbols can also include equality.

These comparisons become the decision points in if statements.

slides.title: Code: compare values
slides.transcript:
Let’s test a few comparisons.

Sales is one thousand and target is eight hundred. One thousand is greater than eight hundred, so the first result should be True. Sales is not equal to target, so the equality check should be False. Sales is different from target, so the final comparison should be True.

[tts-break]

Run the cell and confirm those predictions. Then change sales to eight hundred. Notice which answers flip.

This is the basic building block for every decision we write later.

slides.title: The if statement runs only when true
slides.transcript:
An if statement runs its indented block only when the condition is true.

Sales is one thousand and the condition asks whether sales is greater than eight hundred. Because that is true, Python prints “Good sales day.” Then the program continues and prints “Analysis complete.”

[tts-break]

Now imagine sales were seven hundred. The indented line would be skipped, but “Analysis complete” would still run because it is outside the if block.

Indentation is not decoration in Python. It defines which lines belong to the decision.

slides.title: if / else chooses between two paths
slides.transcript:
Use if and else when exactly one of two outcomes should happen.

Here sales is seven hundred. The condition asks whether sales is greater than eight hundred. That is false, so Python skips the if block and runs the else block instead.

[tts-break]

Change sales to nine hundred and run the cell again. Now the first branch should run.

This two-way pattern appears everywhere: pass or fail, valid or invalid, above target or below target, approved or not approved.

slides.title: elif handles several categories
slides.transcript:
Sometimes we need more than two outcomes. Elif lets us test several rules in order.

With a score of eighty-six, the first condition—score at least ninety—is false. Python then checks score at least eighty, which is true, so it prints “Good” and stops checking the remaining branches.

[tts-break]

Order matters because the first true branch wins. For threshold categories, it is often easiest to check from the highest threshold downward.

Try scores of ninety-five, eighty-five, seventy-five, and sixty. Trace which branch should run before executing the code.

slides.title: Combine rules with Boolean logic
slides.transcript:
Real decisions often depend on more than one condition. That is where and, or, and not become useful.

For a bonus, both sales above one thousand and returns below fifty must be true. That is an and condition. For “needs attention,” either low sales or high returns is enough, so or makes sense.

The not operator reverses a Boolean result.

[tts-break]

Read these expressions as plain language first. If you can explain the business rule clearly, the Python usually becomes much easier to write.

slides.title: Common beginner mistakes
slides.transcript:
Most early control-flow errors are structural rather than mathematical.

A single equals sign assigns a value; double equals compares values. If statements need a colon at the end of the condition. The lines controlled by the statement must be indented consistently.

[tts-break]

A useful debugging trick is to read the code out loud: “If this is true, do this; otherwise, do that.” If the spoken logic sounds wrong, the code probably needs attention too.

slides.title: For loops repeat over a sequence
slides.transcript:
A for loop is a natural choice when you already have a collection of items to process.

The customers list contains Ava, Ben, and Carla. Python takes the first value, stores it temporarily in customer, runs the indented block, then moves to the next value.

[tts-break]

Read the loop as “for each customer in customers.” That plain-language reading often makes loops easier to understand.

This pattern scales well: the same block can process three records or three thousand records.

slides.title: range() creates a simple count
slides.transcript:
Range is useful when the repetition is based on numbers rather than an existing list.

Range five produces zero, one, two, three, and four. The stop value is not included. Range one to six produces one through five, and a third argument can control the step size.

[tts-break]

The important detail is that Python often starts counting at zero. That may feel unusual at first, but it appears throughout indexing, loops, and many libraries.

slides.title: Running totals are a core analytics pattern
slides.transcript:
A running total uses an accumulator—a variable that starts with an initial value and is updated during each repetition.

Total begins at zero. The loop adds one hundred, then two hundred, then one hundred fifty. The running values become one hundred, three hundred, and finally four hundred fifty.

[tts-break]

This pattern is extremely common. Counters, sums, running balances, and category totals all use the same basic idea: initialize, update, finish.

slides.title: enumerate() gives position and value
slides.transcript:
Sometimes we need both the item and its position. Enumerate gives us both at the same time.

Here the customers are Ava, Ben, and Carla. Because start equals one, the output uses human-friendly numbering: one Ava, two Ben, three Carla.

[tts-break]

This is useful in reports, ranked lists, and any output where the position matters as much as the value.

slides.title: while loops repeat until a condition changes
slides.transcript:
A while loop keeps repeating as long as its condition remains true.

Count begins at five. Each repetition prints the current count and subtracts one. Eventually count reaches zero, the condition count greater than zero becomes false, and the loop stops.

[tts-break]

Whenever you write a while loop, ask one safety question: what changes inside the loop so it can eventually end?

If nothing changes the condition, you may accidentally create an infinite loop.

slides.title: while loops can model changing processes
slides.transcript:
While loops are especially useful when the stopping point depends on a changing value rather than a known number of items.

In the first example, balance starts at one hundred and decreases by twenty until it reaches zero. In the second, visits begins at one and doubles until it is no longer below eight.

[tts-break]

A useful rule of thumb is: use for when the items are known; use while when the stopping condition depends on how a value changes over time.

slides.title: break and continue change loop behavior
slides.transcript:
Break and continue let us change the normal flow of a loop.

Continue skips the rest of the current repetition and moves to the next one. In the first example, the number two is skipped.

Break exits the loop completely. In the second example, once the number reaches four, the loop stops immediately.

[tts-break]

These tools are useful, but use them carefully. If a loop becomes hard to follow, simpler logic is usually better.

slides.title: Combine loops and decisions
slides.transcript:
Most useful data-processing code combines repetition with a decision inside the loop.

The loop takes one sale at a time. The if statement checks whether that sale is at least one thousand. Each value is then labeled as either target met or below target.

[tts-break]

This is a classic classification pattern: iterate over records, apply the same rule, and produce a category for each observation.

slides.title: Nested loops: a loop inside a loop
slides.transcript:
A nested loop means one loop runs inside another.

The outer loop controls rows. For each row, the inner loop goes through three columns. That creates six row-column combinations in total.

[tts-break]

Nested loops are useful for grids, pairwise combinations, and some matrix-style tasks. But readability drops quickly when too many loops are nested, so keep the structure as simple as possible.

slides.title: Analytics example: classify sales days
slides.transcript:
This example brings several ideas together in one small report.

We start with six daily sales values and three counters: low, target, and high. Each sale is checked. Values below one thousand increase the low counter. Values up to eighteen hundred increase the target counter. Anything larger increases the high counter.

[tts-break]

For the current data, expect two low days, three target days, and one high day.

Notice the pattern: initialize counters, loop through the values, classify each one, and update the correct counter. This is a very reusable analytics structure.

slides.title: Count values that meet a condition
slides.transcript:
Counting matches is another common pattern.

The counter starts at zero. Each measurement is checked against ninety-eight point six. When the condition is true, the counter increases by one.

[tts-break]

With the current values, ninety-nine point four and one hundred point two are above the threshold, so the final count should be two.

The exact threshold can represent anything: response time, sales amount, temperature, score, or another business rule.

slides.title: Final activity: simple customer flags
slides.transcript:
This activity combines a loop, several conditions, a counter, and readable output.

A customer becomes priority when spending is at least two hundred fifty and visits are at least three. If that is not true but spending is at least one hundred, the customer is standard. Otherwise the label is follow up.

[tts-break]

Trace the three customers one at a time. Carla should meet the priority rule. Ava spends two hundred forty, so she does not reach the priority spending threshold. Ben falls into the follow-up category.

Also notice the priority counter. It summarizes how many customers met the highest-level rule.

slides.title: Practice prompts for class
slides.transcript:
Use these tasks to practice the patterns rather than copy a finished solution.

Start with a simple threshold check, then build a two-way decision, then a short range loop. After that, count how many values exceed ten and classify values into low, medium, or high categories.

[tts-break]

For the final question, explain in your own words when a while loop makes more sense than a for loop. If you can explain the decision clearly, you are understanding the concept rather than memorizing syntax.

slides.title: Self-check
slides.transcript:
Before finishing, check whether you can trace control flow without running the code.

Can you tell when a condition is true or false? Can you identify the indented block controlled by an if statement? Can you follow one repetition of a loop at a time?

[tts-break]

For while loops, make sure you can point to the value that changes and eventually stops the loop. For analytics, make sure you can recognize the classify, count, flag, and summarize patterns.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let’s summarize the module.

Conditions produce True or False. If, elif, and else choose among paths. For loops repeat over known items or counts. While loops repeat until a condition changes. Break stops a loop and continue skips a repetition.

[tts-break]

Together, these tools let us classify, count, flag, and summarize observations.

Next, functions will help us package repeated logic into reusable pieces of code.

[tts-break]

Module 3 takes the logic you just practiced and makes it reusable. Instead of rewriting the same decision or calculation in several places, you’ll learn how to package that work inside functions, pass values into them, return results, and build cleaner analytical code.
